title: Japan's 10 Most Remarkable Ancient Trees
seo_title: The 10 Most Famous Ancient Trees in Japan
meta_description: Ten ancient trees in Japan worth the journey: Jomon Sugi, a camphor 24 metres round, the first cherries Japan protected, and a camphor you walk through.
intro: Japan keeps its oldest trees where it keeps its gods. Seven of these ten stand on shrine or temple ground, one in a World Heritage forest, and most were worshipped long before anybody measured them. That is why so many of the ages below are traditions rather than findings: a hollow cedar or camphor cannot be cored to the middle, so the number is what the shrine says, and each entry tells you which kind of number it is. What can be measured is the body, and here the figures are enormous: three trunks come close to twenty metres round or pass it. The order is ours, weighing age where a source gives one, girth and height where somebody has taped them, and how widely the tree is known. The last entry is the youngest by far, and it is here for a distance rather than an age.

entries.note: The largest yakusugi known, 16.4 metres round, found only in 1966 by a postal worker. Published ages run from 1,300 years to 7,200 because the trunk is hollow and nobody has reached its oldest wood; the Ministry of the Environment says over 2,600. Budget a full mountain day, nine to ten hours on foot there and back.

The thickest trunk we map in Japan, 24.22 metres round, ranked first in the country by the Environment Agency's 1988 survey of giant trees. It was already a sacred tree when the shrine beside it was founded in 1123, which puts it at 900 years at the very least. It stands in Aira, a day trip north of Kagoshima.

A camphor 20 metres round with a small stone shrine standing inside its hollow trunk. Takeo Shrine gives it 3,000 years, which is tradition rather than a measurement. Since 2022 you look at it from a few metres back while its roots recover.

Two cedar trunks from one base, the taller about 60 metres, on the grounds of Yasaka Shrine. It has been a Special Natural Monument since 1952, and the railway station 800 metres away is named after it. The 200 yen entry pays towards protecting the ground its roots run under.

One of five single trees on Japan's very first list of National Natural Monuments, in 1922, and one of the Three Great Cherry Trees. The 1,800 to 2,000 years is a legend tied to the prince Yamato Takeru. It grows outward rather than up, a root flare near twelve metres round under a tree about ten metres tall, with pale blossom in early April.

A camphor you walk through: its split base forms a passage seven metres long that worshippers used on the way to the inner sanctuary of Oyamazumi Shrine. Its own believers nearly killed it in the Meiji era by stripping its bark as a charm for long life, and it regrew from its own roots. Free, and a short detour off the Shimanami Kaido.

Inspected in 1948 and given three years to live, then saved by a Gifu dentist who spent a month grafting new roots onto it. The name means pale ink, for blossom that opens white and fades to grey in early April. Another of the Three Great Cherry Trees, protected the same day as Jindai-zakura.

A ginkgo 42.5 metres tall, said to have grown from the walking stick of Honen, the founder of Pure Land Buddhism, planted at the temple gate when he was a boy. In 2013 DNA tests linked it to two other ginkgos in the same story, which corroborates the legend without dating the tree. The temple lights it after dark.

Legend says it flew overnight from Kyoto to follow the exiled courtier Sugawara no Michizane in 901. It flowers first of the roughly six thousand plums at Dazaifu Tenmangu, usually from late January, and students touch it for luck before exams. Thirty minutes by train from central Fukuoka.

No registered A-bombed tree in Hiroshima stood closer to the hypocentre: 370 metres. It was never transplanted, which is what the letter a in its register code N03a1-01 records, so it stands exactly where it stood on 6 August 1945. Free, in the Chuo Park green space.
